title: Lab 5: Count Regression
text: This report applies a count-regression workflow to investigate the factors associated with how often older adults visit a physician’s office. Rather than fitting a single model, it builds up a Poisson model, checks it with simulation-based residuals, moves to a negative binomial (NB) model, decides whether the zeros need their own model, and then tests and probes an interaction.

title: Lab 5: Count Regression

The outcome is a count: visits are whole numbers, bounded at zero, and strongly right-skewed, with most people reporting a handful of visits and a long tail of frequent visitors. The variance (45.69) is about 7.9 times the mean (5.77), far from the equality a Poisson model assumes, so overdispersion is expected. About 15.5% of people had no visits at all, which we will need to check against what each model predicts. There are also some unusually large counts: the maximum is 89 visits, while 99% of people had 31 or fewer, leaving 43 people above that value. These extreme values are plausible for an older, chronically ill population, but they will pull a linear model and inflate the variance.

title: Lab 5: Count Regression
text:
2. Specify competing count models

2.1. Why not a linear model?









DHARMa simulates new datasets from the fitted model and asks where each observed value falls among the simulations; if the model is correct, these scaled residuals are uniform, the QQ plot follows the diagonal, and the residual-versus-predicted plot is flat. The Gaussian model fails these checks. The QQ plot follows an S-shaped curve rather than the diagonal, the Kolmogorov–Smirnov test of uniformity is significant (p < .001), and the outlier test flags many observations that fall outside every simulated value. In the residual-versus-predicted plot, the residuals are not a flat, even band: they have a curved lower edge, because people cannot make fewer than zero visits, and a cluster of extreme high values. The model therefore gets the shape of the outcome’s distribution wrong in a systematic way. The deeper problems go beyond the plot. A linear model treats visits as a continuous, unbounded outcome, so it can predict impossible negative counts (here the lowest fitted value is -0.28). It assumes constant variance, but the spread of counts grows with their mean. It also treats effects as additive, when it is more natural for something like an extra chronic condition to multiply the expected number of visits. Together, these problems make both the coefficients and their standard errors unreliable.

title: Lab 5: Count Regression
text:
3. Evaluate the Poisson model

3.1. Simulate residuals











3.2. Test for overdispersion and excess zeros


















3.3. Interpret the diagnostics
The DHARMa plots show that the full Poisson model fits poorly: the QQ plot bends sharply away from the diagonal, and the residuals pile up at the extremes of the 0–1 range across the predicted values, meaning the observed counts are more spread out than the model’s simulations. The formal tests confirm this. The dispersion ratio is 7.25 (p < .001), so the observed variance is several times what the Poisson expects, and there are 15.03 times as many zeros as the Poisson predicts (p < .001). Overdispersion matters because the Poisson’s standard errors are derived from the assumption that the variance equals the mean. When the real variance is larger, the standard errors are too small, the confidence intervals too narrow, and the p-values too optimistic, so predictors can look more precisely estimated than they are. We should not move straight to a zero-inflated model on the basis of this zero-inflation test, because overdispersion and excess zeros are linked. A model that allows extra variance, such as the negative binomial, also predicts more zeros, so the apparent excess may disappear once the dispersion is handled. The zero test should be re-run on the NB2 before deciding that the zeros need their own process.

title: Lab 5: Count Regression
section: 4. Fit and evaluate a negative binomial model
text:
4. Fit and evaluate a negative binomial model

4.1. Estimate the NB2 model


4.2. Compare the Poisson and NB2
The NB2 fit significantly better than the full Poisson model, χ²(1) = 12129.08, p < .001. The test has 1 degree of freedom because the two models share the same six predictors and intercept; the NB2 adds only one parameter, the dispersion parameter (θ), which lets the variance grow faster than the mean. The Poisson is the special case where that extra variance is zero, which is why the two models are nested.
The NB2 resolved the overdispersion (see 4.3), but a moderate excess of zeros remains. What matters for interpretation is what this means for the Poisson’s conclusions. The coefficients are similar in both models, so the direction and rough size of each association do not change. However, the NB2’s standard errors are between 2.0 and 2.8 times larger than the Poisson’s. The Poisson was therefore overstating the precision of every estimate by a wide margin. In this large sample all predictors remain significant in the NB2, but the Poisson’s small p-values and narrow confidence intervals were not trustworthy, and in a smaller sample the same overconfidence could easily have produced false positives.


4.3. Re-check the NB2 with DHARMa























The NB2 resolved the overdispersion: the dispersion ratio is now 1.04 (p = .432), close to 1 and non-significant, and the QQ plot sits much closer to the diagonal. However, the zero-inflation test is still significant: there are 1.10 times as many zeros as the NB2 expects (p < .001). The NB2’s extra variance accounts for most of the zeros, but not all of them.


4.4. Visualize predicted counts
This plot shows predicted visits on the count scale across the number of chronic conditions, holding the other predictors at their reference levels (average health, male, no insurance) or mean (school).









The line curves upward even though the model is linear in its predictors. That is the log link: each additional chronic condition adds a constant amount to the log of the expected count, which multiplies the expected count by the same factor (here about 1.22). The same one-condition increase therefore adds more visits when the expected count is already high, so the curve gets steeper as the number of chronic conditions rises.

5. Decide whether the zeros need their own model

5.1. Make the decision
The NB2 zero-inflation test in 4.3 was significant, with a ratio above 1 (1.10), so the NB2 underpredicts the zeros. A zero-inflated NB (ZINB) and a hurdle NB were fit with the same five predictors in both the count and zero parts.
The hurdle is not nested in the NB2, so the three models are compared with information criteria (lower is better).

5.2. Justify your choice
The hurdle NB appears to be the most appropriate model. The NB2’s zero-inflation test showed that it underpredicts the number of people with no visits (ratio = 1.10, p < .001), so the zeros do need their own modelling. Adding a zero part clearly helps: the ZINB fit significantly better than the NB2, χ²(7) = 143.14, p < .001. Between the two zero models, the hurdle NB had the lowest AIC (24330.41, vs. 24340.77 for the ZINB and 24469.91 for the NB2) and the lowest BIC (24426.27, vs. 24436.63 and 24521.03), even though the ZINB and hurdle have the same number of parameters. Re-checking the hurdle with DHARMa shows that it reproduces the observed zeros almost exactly (ratio = 1.00, p = 1.000). This is expected, since a hurdle model fits the zero/non-zero split directly. Its dispersion test is significant (ratio = 1.15, p < .001), but the ratio is close to 1 and, with 4,406 observations, even small deviations reach significance, so this is a minor misfit rather than a reason to reject the model. The hurdle structure is also substantively interpretable: deciding whether to see a physician at all is plausibly a different process from how many visits someone makes once they are in the health-care system.

title: Lab 5: Count Regression
text:
6. Test and probe an interaction
Question: Does the association between the number of chronic conditions and physician visits differ for people with and without private insurance?

6.1. State your prediction
I expect insurance to moderate the association between chronic conditions and visits. People without private insurance may be more reluctant to go to the doctor because of out-of-pocket costs, so additional chronic conditions should translate into fewer extra visits for them. The slope of chronic conditions should therefore be steeper for people with insurance than for people without it.


6.2. Fit the interaction model
The selected hurdle model is re-estimated with chronic * insurance in place of the separate chronic and insurance terms, in both the count and zero parts, keeping health, gender, and school as controls.


6.3. Test whether the interaction is needed
Adding the chronic × insurance interaction did not improve fit over the additive hurdle model, χ²(2) = 0.46, p = .793. The test has 2 degrees of freedom because the product term was added to both parts of the hurdle model. The interaction model also has a higher AIC (24333.94 vs. 24330.41) and BIC (24442.59 vs. 24426.27). The omnibus test only says whether the interaction terms improve fit overall. Further probing shows what the chronic-conditions slope actually is within each insurance group, and how large the insurance difference is at specific numbers of chronic conditions. That tells us whether a null interaction reflects two genuinely similar slopes, and whether insurance still matters as a main effect.


6.4. Plot predicted counts









The two lines are almost parallel on the log scale: insured people are predicted to make more visits at every number of chronic conditions, but the rate at which visits rise with chronic conditions looks very similar in the two groups.


6.5. Probe the interaction

Simple slopes
The pairs() comparison of the slopes reproduces the count-part interaction coefficient from summary(interact). The estimate is 0.0164 (SE = 0.0282, p = .560), compared with the interaction coefficient of -0.0164 (SE = 0.0282, p = .560). The standard error and p-value are identical, and the estimate is the same size with the sign flipped. The sign flips because pairs() computes the first level minus the second (no − yes), whereas the interaction coefficient is the change in the chronic slope for the non-reference group (yes − no). With a two-level moderator, these are the same question. There are only two slopes, so “do the slopes differ?” is answered by a single difference, and the product term is that difference.


Simple effects
Why don’t these counts match the plot exactly? ggeffects holds health and gender at their reference levels (average health, male), while emmeans averages over the levels of health and gender. Both are valid; they answer slightly different questions about what a “typical” person is. The insurance contrasts are the same either way. Health and gender do not interact with insurance, so their effects add the same amount to both insurance groups on the log scale and cancel out of the difference.

6.7. Interpret the interaction
There is no evidence that the association between chronic conditions and visits differs by insurance status. Among people with at least one visit, the chronic-conditions slope was 0.160 without insurance and 0.143 with insurance, a difference that was small and non-significant (p = .560). The zero part showed the same pattern, with a non-significant interaction (p = .725). My prediction was therefore not supported: insured people did not show a steeper slope. I am confident in this null result, given its consistency across the evidence. The omnibus LRT was far from significant, the interaction raised both AIC and BIC, the two simple slopes were nearly identical and both clearly positive, and the simple effects show a roughly constant insurance gap across low, average, and high numbers of chronic conditions. The probing does show that insurance matters, but as a main effect rather than a moderator: insured people make more visits at every level of chronic conditions, by about the same proportional amount.

title: Lab 5: Count Regression
section: 7. Write up and discuss your findings
text:
7. Write up and discuss your findings

7.1. Results write-up
Physician office visits were overdispersed (M = 5.77, s² = 45.69; 15.5% zeros). Simulation-based residual checks on the full Poisson model showed significant overdispersion (dispersion ratio = 7.25, p < .001) and excess zeros (observed/expected = 15.03, p < .001). A negative binomial (NB2) model fit significantly better, χ²(1) = 12129.08, p < .001, and resolved the overdispersion (ratio = 1.04, p = .432), but it still underpredicted zeros (ratio = 1.10, p < .001). A separate model for the zeros was therefore needed. A zero-inflated NB improved on the NB2, χ²(7) = 143.14, p < .001, and a hurdle NB had the lowest AIC (24330.41) and BIC (24426.27) of the three models. It reproduced the observed zeros (ratio = 1.00, p = 1.000), so it was retained as the final model.
In the hurdle model, the zero part predicts the log-odds of having no visits, and the count part predicts the number of visits among people with at least one visit; each part holds the other predictors constant. People with more chronic conditions were less likely to have no visits (b = -0.56, 95% CI [-0.65, -0.47], p < .001) and, among visitors, made more visits (b = 0.15, 95% CI [0.12, 0.17], p < .001). Compared with average health, poor health was not associated with having any visits (b = -0.05, 95% CI [-0.36, 0.26], p = .754) but was associated with more visits among visitors (b = 0.38, 95% CI [0.29, 0.48], p < .001). Excellent health was associated with a higher likelihood of no visits (b = 0.31, 95% CI [0.03, 0.59], p = .030) and fewer visits among visitors (b = -0.37, 95% CI [-0.50, -0.24], p < .001). Women were less likely than men to have no visits (b = -0.40, 95% CI [-0.57, -0.23], p < .001), but did not differ from men in the number of visits among visitors (b = 0.06, 95% CI [-0.01, 0.12], p = .088). Each additional year of schooling was associated with a lower likelihood of no visits (b = -0.058, 95% CI [-0.082, -0.035], p < .001) and more visits among visitors (b = 0.021, 95% CI [0.012, 0.030], p < .001). Privately insured people were less likely to have no visits (b = -0.75, 95% CI [-0.94, -0.55], p < .001) and made more visits among visitors (b = 0.13, 95% CI [0.05, 0.22], p = .003). The only non-significant associations were poor health in the zero part and gender in the count part.
Adding a chronic conditions × insurance interaction to both parts of the hurdle model did not significantly improve fit, χ²(2) = 0.46, p = .793. In the count part, chronic conditions were positively associated with visits both for people without insurance (b = 0.16, 95% CI [0.11, 0.21], p < .001) and for people with insurance (b = 0.14, 95% CI [0.12, 0.17], p < .001). Simple effects showed that people without insurance made fewer visits than insured people at low (−1 SD; b = -0.16, p = .014), average (b = -0.14, p = .002), and high (+1 SD; b = -0.11, p = .028) numbers of chronic conditions. Overall, the insurance gap was present and of similar size at every level of chronic conditions, showing an additive effect of insurance rather than a moderated one.


7.2. Discussion
Chronic conditions were the most consistent and important predictor of physician use. They were strongly related both to whether older adults saw a physician at all and to how often they went, with each additional condition multiplying the expected number of visits among visitors by about 1.16. Self-perceived health played a different role. Poor health did not change whether someone had any visits, but it was associated with substantially more visits among those who went, suggesting that perceived health matters mainly for the intensity of care once someone is in the health-care system. Private insurance, gender, and schooling mattered most for the zero part, that is, for whether someone saw a physician at all. This pattern is consistent with access and help-seeking barriers operating mainly at the decision to seek care, while need (chronic conditions and poor health) drives how much care is used.
The analysis has several limitations. The data are cross-sectional and observational, so these associations cannot be interpreted causally; insurance status in particular is likely confounded with income, wealth, and other factors not included in the model. Health is self-reported and coarse, and chronic conditions are a simple count that treats all conditions as equivalent. The data are from 1987–1988 and from US adults aged 66 and older, almost all of whom had Medicare, so “insurance” here means supplementary private coverage, and the findings may not generalize to other ages, health-care systems, or the present day. Finally, the final hurdle model still showed slight residual overdispersion, and the very large counts in the tail may have some influence on the count-part estimates.

5. Nested Model Comparisons
We will evaluate the models. Our main performance metrics are:

AIC: Evaluates model fit while penalizing model complexity. Lower values indicate a preferred balance between fit and complexity.
BIC: Similar to AIC, but applies a stronger penalty for model complexity. Lower values are preferred.
Likelihood-ratio test (χ²): Tests whether adding predictors significantly improves model fit relative to the preceding model. A statistically significant p-value (p < .05) indicates that the additional predictors improve model fit.


5.1. Compare the models
Because our models are nested and estimated using the same observations, we can compare all three models in a single anova() call.
Each row represents a model. We can retain and rename the statistics relevant to our comparison table.


5.2. Extract overall model performance
The glance() function from the broom.mixed package returns a one-row data frame containing model-level statistics.
We can apply it to each fitted model.
We can then combine these results using rbind().


5.3. Combine nested tests and model performance
Because the rows in glances and tests represent the same models in the same order, we can combine them using cbind().

8b. Visualize predicted counts
Coefficients on the log scale are hard to picture, so it helps to plot what the model predicts on the count scale. Here we plot predicted article counts across mentor productivity, holding the other predictors at their reference levels (Men, Single) or means (kid5, phd).









The line curves upward even though the model is linear in its predictors. That’s the log link: each additional mentor article adds a constant amount on the log scale, which multiplies the expected count, so the same one-article increase adds more articles when the expected count is already high.

title: Count Regression: Workflow
section: 9. Do the zeros need their own model?
text:
9. Do the zeros need their own model?
Count data often have lots of zeros, but that alone doesn’t mean you need a special model for them. The question is whether there are more zeros than your model predicts.
We already answered that in 8a. The NB’s zero-inflation test showed the model reproduces the observed zeros well (observed/expected = 0.99, p = 0.772). The NB’s extra variance is enough to generate this many zeros, so a separate model for zeros isn’t needed here, and we continue with the NB2.
If DHARMa had flagged excess zeros after the NB, there are two families of models that give the zeros their own process:

Zero-inflated (ZIP/ZINB): a mixture. Some zeros are “structural” (e.g., a student who would never publish), and the rest come from the count distribution, which can also produce zeros.
Hurdle: a two-part model. One part decides zero vs. non-zero (“did they publish at all?”), and a truncated count distribution handles everything above zero (“if so, how much?”).

Here’s the code you’d use. It isn’t run in this document.
Here a zero inflation model was not necessary.

title: Count Regression: Workflow
text:
11. Results write-up
Article counts were overdispersed (M = 1.69, s² = 3.71; 30% zeros). Simulation-based residual checks on a Poisson model showed significant overdispersion (dispersion ratio = 1.99, p < .001) and excess zeros (observed/expected = 1.44, p < .001). A negative binomial model fit significantly better, χ²(1) = 180.20, p < .001, and showed no remaining evidence of overdispersion (ratio = 1.05, p = .556) or excess zeros (ratio = 0.99, p = .772), so no separate model for zeros was needed.
Holding other predictors constant, women published fewer articles than men (b = −0.22, 95% CI [−0.36, −0.07], p = .003). Each additional child aged 5 or younger was associated with fewer articles (b = −0.18, 95% CI [−0.28, −0.07], p < .001), and each additional mentor article with more articles (b = 0.029, 95% CI [0.023, 0.035], p < .001). Marital status (b = 0.15, 95% CI [−0.01, 0.31], p = .067) and PhD prestige (b = 0.02, 95% CI [−0.06, 0.09], p = .672) were not significantly associated with article counts.
Adding a PhD prestige × gender interaction did not significantly improve fit, χ²(1) = 3.73, p = .053. Simple slopes showed that prestige was not significantly associated with article counts for men (b = −0.04, 95% CI [−0.14, 0.05], p = .363) or women (b = 0.10, 95% CI [−0.01, 0.20], p = .084). Simple effects, however, showed that the gender gap narrowed as prestige increased. Men were expected to publish more articles than women at low prestige (−1 SD; b = 0.36, p < .001) and at average prestige (b = 0.22, p = .002), but the difference was not significant at high prestige (+1 SD; b = 0.09, p = .354).
